rules.title: Written Workplace Violence Prevention Plan (SB 553) since July 1, 2024
rules.plain_english: Covered employers must establish, implement and maintain an effective written Workplace Violence Prevention Plan (WVPP), either stand-alone or as a separate section of the IIPP, specific to each work area and operation. Required elements include responsible persons, employee involvement, coordination with other employers, compliance, communication, reporting without retaliation, emergency response, training, hazard identification and correction, post-incident investigation, and periodic review.
rules.applies_to: All California employers, places of employment and employer-provided housing, except Labor Code 6401.9(b)(2) exemptions (construction employers are covered)
rules.quote: On September 30, 2023, California Senate Bill 553 (Cortese) was signed into law and California Labor Code section 6401.9 will be in effect and enforceable on July 1, 2024. Employers that fall within the scope of this law must establish, implement, and maintain an effective written Workplace Violence Prevention Plan
rules.notes: Read from official Cal/OSHA (dir.ca.gov) guidance pages summarizing LC 6401.9; leginfo.legislature.ca.gov statute text was not reachable from this environment. As of the 2026-10-27 DIR rulemaking page, the implementing regulation (proposed 8 CCR 3343) was still a discussion draft (OSHSB deadline to adopt: 2026-12-31). Re-check for an adopted 3343 in 2027.

rules.title: Violent incident log for every workplace violence incident
rules.plain_english: Record every workplace violence incident (including threats) in a violent incident log, with no personal identifying information. On multi-employer sites, the model plan also has you give a copy of the log to the controlling employer.
rules.applies_to: All California employers, places of employment and employer-provided housing, except Labor Code 6401.9(b)(2) exemptions (construction employers are covered)
rules.quote: All workplace violence incidents are required to be documented in the violent incident log.
rules.notes: Cal/OSHA FAQ (official dir.ca.gov). Employers may design their own log if it captures the LC 6401.9(d)(2) fields. Multi-employer provision is from Cal/OSHA's Model WVPP (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dosh/dosh_publications/Model-WPV-Plan-General-Industry.docx).

rules.title: Workplace violence training: initial and annually
rules.plain_english: Provide WVPP training when the plan is first established, annually thereafter, and when new hazards are identified or the plan changes. Training had to be in place by July 1, 2024.
rules.applies_to: All California employers, places of employment and employer-provided housing, except Labor Code 6401.9(b)(2) exemptions (construction employers are covered)
rules.quote: Annually to ensure all employees understand and comply with the plan.
rules.notes: Quote is from Cal/OSHA's official Model WVPP (dir.ca.gov). The statutory 'initial training ... and annually thereafter' wording also appears as baseline LC 6401.9 text in DIR's draft comparison document (https://www.dir.ca.gov/dosh/doshreg/Workplace-Violence-in-General-Industry/WPV-Draft-Revisions-May-13-2025.docx). FAQ Q21 confirms training was enforceable July 1, 2024 with no grace period.
rules.correction: Not refuted. The statutory wording, taken from the unformatted (baseline LC 6401.9) runs of DIR's comparison document, is: "initial training when the plan is first established, and annually thereafter" plus additional training "when a new or previously unrecognized workplace violence hazard has been identified and when changes are made to the plan". FAQ: 6401.9(b)-(g) enforceable July 1, 2024. Caveat: leginfo was not reachable, so the statute was seen only through DIR's verbatim reproduction.

rules.title: Workplace violence records: 5 years (training 1 year)
rules.plain_english: Keep workplace violence hazard identification/evaluation/correction records, violent incident logs, and incident investigation records for at least 5 years; keep WVPP training records for at least 1 year. Records must not contain medical information.
rules.applies_to: All California employers, places of employment and employer-provided housing, except Labor Code 6401.9(b)(2) exemptions (construction employers are covered)
rules.quote: Records of workplace violence hazard identification, evaluation, and correction, for a minimum of five years.
rules.notes: Same DIR page lists, as separate bullets: training records minimum one year; Violence Incident Logs minimum five years; incident investigation records minimum five years. Official Cal/OSHA guidance page summarizing LC 6401.9(f); training records must include dates, contents/summary, trainer names and qualifications, and attendee names and job titles (per DIR draft baseline text and Model WVPP).

rules.title: Give employees WVPP records within 15 calendar days
rules.plain_english: Workplace violence hazard records, training records and violent incident logs must be made available to employees and their representatives on request, free, for examination and copying within 15 calendar days.

parameters.division_access: all WVP records incl. investigations upon request

rules.applies_to: All California employers, places of employment and employer-provided housing, except Labor Code 6401.9(b)(2) exemptions (construction employers are covered)
rules.quote: All records of workplace violence hazard identification, evaluation, and correction, as well as training records and violent incident logs, shall be made available to employees and their authorized representatives, upon request and without cost, for examination and copying within 15 calendar days of a request.
rules.correction: Not refuted. The 15 calendar days and no-cost access match the baseline LC 6401.9 text in DIR's comparison document. Wording note: the statutory baseline reads "employees and their representatives". The quote, from DIR's web page, says "their authorized representatives", and "authorized employee" is a proposed 3343 addition. The quote is accurate to its cited DIR page. Leginfo was not reachable.

rules.title: Review the WVPP at least annually and after incidents
rules.plain_english: Review the Workplace Violence Prevention Plan for effectiveness at least annually, when a deficiency becomes apparent, and after a workplace violence incident.
rules.applies_to: All California employers, places of employment and employer-provided housing, except Labor Code 6401.9(b)(2) exemptions (construction employers are covered)
rules.quote: At least annually. When a deficiency is observed or becomes apparent. After a workplace violence incident.
rules.notes: Read in Cal/OSHA's official Model WVPP; DIR's draft-vs-statute comparison shows the same 'annually, when a deficiency is observed or becomes apparent, and after a workplace incident' review language.
rules.correction: Not refuted. The baseline LC 6401.9 text reads: "The plan shall be reviewed at least: annually, when a deficiency is observed or becomes apparent, and after a workplace incident." The Model WVPP quote matches. Leginfo was not reachable.

rules.title: Workplace violence injury: workers' comp notice within one working day
rules.plain_english: If an employee is the victim of a crime at the workplace (which covers many workplace violence incidents), give them written notice that they may be eligible for workers' compensation, including for psychiatric injuries. Deliver it personally or by first-class mail within one working day of the crime, or of the date the employer reasonably should have known of it. Also log the incident, investigate, report serious injuries within 8 hours, and record it on the Form 300 if recordable.

parameters.trigger: employee is the victim of a crime that occurred at the employee's place of employment
parameters.notice_form: written notice of workers' compensation eligibility, including for psychiatric injuries resulting from the crime
clock_starts_from: date the employer reasonably should have known of the crime

rules.applies_to: All California employers, places of employment and employer-provided housing, except Labor Code 6401.9(b)(2) exemptions (construction employers are covered)
rules.quote: Employers must give employees notice of workers' compensation eligibility within one working day of a workplace violence incident.
rules.notes: The CSLB Law Book (PDF p.47) separately notes the Labor Code 3553 duty to notify workplace-crime victims of workers' comp eligibility.
rules.correction: The 1-working-day deadline is confirmed. The trigger was too loose. Labor Code 3553 applies when an employee is the victim of a crime at the place of employment, not to every workplace violence incident, and the employee need not be injured. The notice must be written, covers workers' comp eligibility including psychiatric injuries, and goes out personally or by first-class mail within one working day of the crime or of the date the employer reasonably should have known of it. The DWC FAQ agrees: 'If the employee is the victim of a crime that happened at work, you must give notice of workers' compensation eligibility within one working day of the crime.' Added parameters: trigger, notice_form, delivery_methods and clock_starts_from. plain_english was reworded. The verbatim_quote (DIR General-Industry page) is unchanged. The statute text was seen only as leginfo search excerpts, not as the full page.

rules.title: WVPP exemptions (Labor Code 6401.9(b)(2))
rules.plain_english: Exempt from the WVPP law: health care settings covered by 8 CCR 3342, certain CDCR facilities and POST-certified law enforcement agencies complying with 3203, employees teleworking from a location of their choice not controlled by the employer, and places of employment with fewer than 10 employees working there at any given time that are not accessible to the public and comply with 3203.
rules.applies_to: All California employers, places of employment and employer-provided housing, except Labor Code 6401.9(b)(2) exemptions (construction employers are covered)
rules.quote: Places of employment where there are less than 10 employees working at the place at any given time and that are not accessible to the public, if the places are in compliance with Section 3203 of Title 8 of the California Code of Regulations.
rules.notes: The quoted sentence appears in DIR's official May 13, 2025 draft-revisions comparison document. There it is formatted bold, double-underlined and double-struck, NOT as 'Regular text is Labor Code 6401.9', so that document does not establish it as statute text. Per the DIR WVP FAQ, the exemptions are at LC 6401.9(b)(2)(A)-(F). Leginfo excerpts read on 2026-11-25 (WebSearch restricted to leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) show this sentence verbatim as Labor Code 6401.9(b)(2)(F). Most active construction jobsites are 'accessible to the public' in some sense or exceed 10 workers, so treat the small-site exemption as narrow and something the employer must prove. Proposed 8 CCR 3343 would change the headcount test (draft only).
rules.correction: No parameter changes. In the leginfo excerpts the quoted small-site sentence appears verbatim as LC 6401.9(b)(2)(F): fewer than 10 employees at any given time, not accessible to the public, and in compliance with 8 CCR 3203. They also show the other exemptions: 8 CCR 3342 health care; (C) CDCR facilities that comply with 3203; (D) law enforcement agencies that are a 'department or participating department' under 11 CCR 1001, have POST compliance confirmation, and have all agency facilities in compliance with 3203; and (E) telework from a location of the employee's choice not under employer control. They also show (b)(3), which lets the Division order an otherwise exempt employer or place to comply. The earlier provenance correction to the notes (docx formatting) still stands. The text was seen as search excerpts, not the full page.

rules.title: Cal/OSHA civil penalty amounts (2025 schedule)
rules.plain_english: Cal/OSHA penalties: regulatory and general violations up to $16,285 each; serious violations up to $25,000 (base $18,000); repeat violations multiplied x2/x4/x10 up to $162,851; willful violations multiplied x5 with a minimum of $11,632 and maximum of $162,851.
rules.applies_to: All California employers
rules.quote: Regulatory, General and Serious -- the Proposed Penalty is multiplied by five. However, the penalty for any willful violation shall not be less than $11,632 and shall not exceed $162,851.
rules.notes: Regulatory/general maximum and repeat/willful caps are inflation-adjusted each January 1 (last amendment shown on DIR page: filed 12-19-2024, operative 1-1-2025). Check for a 2026 adjustment before using as a hard cap.
rules.correction: None. The quote and every parameter match the official text re-fetched 2026-11-25. On that date the 336 history still ended at the amendment filed 12-19-2024, operative 1-1-2025, with no 2026 adjustment shown. A WebSearch of dir.ca.gov also found no 1-1-2026 schedule. These are the current published values. Re-check each January for a file-and-print inflation adjustment under Labor Code 6427(b), 6429(a)(2) and 6431(b).

rules.title: No IIPP = serious-violation penalties not reduced (except size)
rules.plain_english: If you do not have an operative IIPP, Cal/OSHA will not reduce penalties for serious violations for good faith or history, only for business size.

parameters.condition: no operative injury prevention program (LC 6401.7)

rules.applies_to: All California employers
rules.quote: (8) Injury Prevention Program -- The penalty for any Serious violation shall not be subject to adjustment pursuant to this subsection other than for Size as set forth in part (1) of this subsection where the employer does not have an operative injury prevention program
rules.correction: None. Quote string-matched against the re-fetched official text and every parameter value checked against it.

rules.title: Submit abatement statement within 10 working days to keep 50% credit
rules.plain_english: To get the 50% abatement credit on a serious violation not abated during the inspection, submit a statement signed under penalty of perjury (with evidence) within 10 working days after the abatement period ends. Missing it rescinds the credit and adds failure-to-abate penalties.

parameters.trigger: end of abatement period fixed in citation

rules.applies_to: Cited employers
rules.quote: The signed statement and supporting evidence must be received within 10 working days after the end of the period fixed in the citation for abatement.
rules.correction: None. Quote string-matched against the re-fetched official text and every parameter value checked against it. Precision note: under 336(f), a missed statement rescinds the abatement credit. The daily failure-to-abate penalty accrues only while the violation actually stays unabated.

rules.title: New employers: 1-year grace for IIPP regulatory/general penalties
rules.plain_english: No civil penalty is assessed against a new employer for a regulatory or general IIPP violation during its first year in California if it made a good-faith effort to comply. Employers who adopt and implement Cal/OSHA's Model IIPP for non-high-hazard employment get no penalty for a first IIPP violation.
rules.applies_to: New employers establishing a business in California
rules.quote: (10) No civil penalty shall be assessed against any new employer for a period of one year after the date the new employer establishes a business in the state for a regulatory or general violation of the Injury and Illness Prevention Program Standard
rules.notes: Construction is generally high-hazard, so the non-high-hazard model-program safe harbor may not apply.

rules.title: CSLB discipline for safety violations (B&P 7109.5)
rules.plain_english: A CSLB licensee can be disciplined for violating tree-work safety orders (8 CCR 3420 et seq.) regardless of injury, or any Labor Code Division 5 (Cal/OSHA) safety provision that results in death or serious injury to an employee. CSLB citation civil penalty range for 7109.5: $500 to $8,000.

parameters.trigger_death_or_serious_injury: any Labor Code Division 5 safety provision

rules.applies_to: CSLB licensees
rules.source: PDF page 351 of the 2026 CSLB Law Book; PDF page 540 of the 2026 CSLB Law Book
rules.quote: (b) Violation of any safety provision in, or authorized by, Division 5 (commencing with Section 6300) of the Labor Code resulting in death or serious injury to an employee constitutes a cause for disciplinary action.
rules.notes: B&P 7110(c): willful/deliberate violation of safety laws is also cause for discipline (CCR 884 range $200-$30,000).

rules.title: Criminal liability: willful violation causing death or prolonged impairment
rules.plain_english: Employers, and employees who have direction, management, control or custody of the employment or of other employees, who willfully violate an occupational safety or health standard that causes an employee's death or permanent or prolonged bodily impairment can be prosecuted by the local district attorney. On conviction the penalty is a fine of up to $250,000, imprisonment of up to 3 years, or both. For a corporation or LLC the fine can be up to $1.5 million.

elements: willful violation of an occupational safety or health standard
causes death of an employee, or permanent or prolonged impairment of the body of an employee
who: employee having direction, management control, or custody of employment
parameters.enforced_by: local district attorney (Cal/OSHA Bureau of Investigations refers cases)
parameters.penalty_amounts_source: DIR, The Guide to Cal/OSHA (Aug 2023) p.13, summarizing Labor Code 6425

rules.applies_to: Employers and supervisors
rules.source: PDF page 49 of the 2026 CSLB Law Book
rules.quote: who willfully violates any occupational safety or health standard that causes the death of any employee or the prolonged impairment of the body of any employee shall, upon conviction, be punished by a fine and or imprisonment
rules.notes: Amounts are from DIR's Guide to Cal/OSHA summary of LC 6425. Leginfo excerpts also show a lower alternative tier: county jail up to 1 year and/or a fine up to $100,000. That tier is not encoded because the full statute text was not seen. The verbatim_quote is the CSLB Law Book narrative, which drops 'permanent'. It is not statute text. Pending change: AB 2321 (2025-26) is reported as chaptered (Ch. 936, approved 2026-09-30). It would extend 6425 to willful violations causing serious injury, illness or exposure. Confirm the final text and operative date before relying on the current elements after 2026.
rules.correction: The harm element was incomplete. LC 6425 covers a willful violation causing death or PERMANENT or prolonged impairment of the body of an employee. The DIR Guide and the leginfo excerpts both say this. The Law Book paraphrase (and the old elements list) said only 'prolonged impairment'. Fixed elements and plain_english. The penalty amounts were missing. Added from DIR's Guide: a fine up to $250,000, imprisonment up to 3 years, or both; for a corporation or LLC a fine up to $1.5 million; enforced by the local DA. The quote is unchanged because it is verbatim to its Law Book source. FLAG, not applied: leginfo search excerpts report AB 2321 (2025-26) as Chapter 936, approved 2026-09-30. It amends 6425 to add serious injury, illness or exposure as a triggering harm. The final status and text were not seen, and the excerpts conflicted.

rules.title: State minimum wage $16.90/hour (2026)
rules.plain_english: Every California employer, no matter how small, must pay at least $16.90 per hour for all hours worked starting January 1, 2026. A higher city or county rate overrides this where the work is done.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Every employer, regardless of the number of employees, shall pay to each employee wages not less than the following: (1) Sixteen dollars and ninety cents ($16.90) per hour for all hours worked, effective January 1, 2026;
rules.notes: Exempt from minimum wage per DLSE FAQ: outside salespersons; parent, spouse or child of the employer; apprentices regularly indentured under the Division of Apprenticeship Standards. Separate higher state rates exist for fast food and health care (not normally construction). Public works projects require prevailing wage instead (separate domain).

rules.title: Higher city/county minimum wage must be paid
rules.plain_english: If the city or county where the employee works has a higher minimum wage than the state, the employer must pay the higher local rate. Many California cities are higher than $16.90.

parameters.local_rate_list_referenced_by_DLSE: UC Berkeley Labor Center inventory of city and county minimum wages (not an official DIR table)

rules.applies_to: Employers with employees working within a city or county that has its own minimum wage ordinance
rules.citation: Labor Code 1182.12; local ordinances (DLSE Minimum Wage FAQ Q3)
rules.quote: if a local entity (city or county) has adopted a higher minimum wage, employees must be paid the local wage where it is higher than the state or federal minimum wage rates.
rules.notes: No local rates were read from official city sources in this pass; a tool must look up the jobsite city/county rate (many adjust each July 1 or January 1). For construction crews moving between jobsites, the rate applies per location where hours are worked (verify each ordinance's coverage threshold, e.g., minimum hours worked in the city).

rules.title: State minimum wage adjusts each year by CPI-W (max 3.5%)
rules.plain_english: The state minimum wage now changes every January 1 based on inflation. It can go up by at most 3.5% in a year and can never go down.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: After the state minimum wage reached $15 an hour, the rate is adjusted annually for inflation based on the national consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers (CPI-W). However, the minimum wage cannot be lowered, even if there is a negative CPI, and the highest raise allowed in any one year is 3.5 percent.
rules.notes: A tool should store rates by effective date and refresh each year from MW-20XX orders published by DIR.

rules.title: Minimum wage applies to all hours in each payroll period, including piece rate
rules.plain_english: For every pay period, total pay must equal at least minimum wage times all hours worked, whether the worker is paid hourly, by the piece (e.g., per square or linear foot) or by commission.
rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: Every employer shall pay to each employee, on the established payday for the period involved, not less than the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked in the payroll period, whether the remuneration is measured by time, piece, commission, or otherwise.
rules.notes: Piece-rate workers also have separate rest/recovery and nonproductive time pay rules (Labor Code 226.2) that were not read in this pass.

rules.title: Learner rate: 85% of minimum wage for first 160 hours
rules.plain_english: Under the IWC wage orders that have a learner clause (for example Order 4, which covers office staff), a new worker with no similar experience may be paid 85% of the minimum wage, rounded to the nearest nickel, for their first 160 hours only. Wage Order 16, which covers on-site construction workers, has no learner rate, so field employees must get the full minimum wage from day one.

parameters.source_orders: IWC Orders 1-15 §4(A) (verified in Order 4-2001); absent from Order 16-2001 and MW-2026

rules.applies_to: New employees with no previous similar or related experience who are covered by an IWC order that contains a learner clause (Orders 1-15, e.g., Order 4 office/clerical staff of a contractor). NOT available for on-site construction, drilling, logging or mining employees covered by IWC Order 16-2001.
rules.citation: IWC Orders 1-15 §4(A) learner clause (e.g., IWC Order 4-2001 §4(A)); DLSE Minimum Wage FAQ Q4. Not in IWC Order 16-2001 §4 or MW-2026.
rules.quote: There is an exception for learners, regardless of age, who may be paid not less than 85 percent of the minimum wage rounded to the nearest nickel during their first 160 hours of employment in occupations in which they have no previous similar or related experience.
rules.notes: Derived rate: 16.90 x 0.85 = 14.365, rounded to nearest nickel = $14.35. Local ordinances may not allow a learner rate; check locally. Verification: WO16 §4(A)-(B) and MW-2026 have no learner clause; Order 4-2001 §4(A) does.
rules.correction: The learner subminimum is in the industry wage orders that contain a learner clause (e.g., IWC Order 4 §4(A)), not in MW-2026. IWC Order 16-2001, which covers on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining, has no learner clause in §4. A construction tool must not apply the 85% rate to WO16 field employees. Corrected the citation, source_location, applies_to and plain_english, and added not_available_under_wage_order_16. The 85%, 160-hour and nearest-nickel figures and the $14.35 derivation are confirmed.

rules.title: Exempt (EAP) salary must be at least 2x minimum wage ($70,304/yr in 2026)
rules.plain_english: To treat a manager, administrator or professional as exempt from overtime and meal/rest rules, they must mainly (over half their time) do exempt duties and earn a salary of at least twice the state minimum wage for 40 hours a week: $5,858.67/month or $70,304/year in 2026.

parameters.primarily_means: more than one-half of work time

rules.applies_to: Executive, administrative and professional employees of construction/drilling/logging/mining employers
rules.quote: No person shall be considered to be employed in an administrative, executive, or professional capacity unless the person is primarily engaged in the duties which meet the test of the exemption, and earns a monthly salary equivalent to not less than two (2) times the state minimum wage for full-time employment.
rules.notes: Dollar figures are computed from the primary rule and the $16.90 state rate (local minimum wages do not change the state exemption threshold). Duties test also required.

rules.title: Employer provides tools unless worker earns 2x minimum wage
rules.plain_english: If tools or equipment are required or needed for the job, the employer must provide and maintain them. Only workers paid at least twice the minimum wage ($33.80/hour in 2026) can be required to bring their own customary hand tools.

parameters.rule: if hourly_rate < 2 * min_wage: employer must provide and maintain all required tools and equipment
parameters.uniforms: required uniforms provided and maintained by employer (WO16 §8(A))

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: When the employer requires the use of tools or equipment or they are necessary for the performance of a job, such tools and equipment shall be provided and maintained by the employer, except that an employee whose wages are at least two (2) times the minimum wage may provide and maintain hand tools and equipment customarily required by the particular trade or craft
rules.notes: Threshold computed from the $16.90 state minimum wage; whether a higher local minimum wage changes the 2x threshold was not verified. Labor Code 2802 expense reimbursement (vehicle, phone) still applies.

rules.title: Maximum meal and lodging credits against minimum wage (2026)
rules.plain_english: An employer may count meals or lodging toward minimum wage only with a voluntary written agreement, and only up to set amounts (for 2026: breakfast $6.10, lunch $8.42, dinner $11.28; private room $79.46/week).

max_credits_2026_usd.apartment_rule: two-thirds of ordinary rental value, not more than max

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001) (e.g., remote jobsite camps)
rules.quote: Meals or lodging may not be credited against the minimum wage without a voluntary written agreement between the employer and the employee.
rules.notes: Signing the 2810.5 Notice to Employee does not count as the voluntary written agreement (per DLSE template).

rules.title: Overtime 1.5x after 8 hours/day, 40 hours/week, and first 8 hours of 7th day
rules.plain_english: Pay time-and-a-half for hours over 8 in a workday (up to 12), over 40 in a workweek, and for the first 8 hours on the seventh consecutive day worked in a workweek.

parameters.workday: any consecutive 24-hour period beginning at the same time each calendar day
parameters.workweek: any 7 consecutive days starting with the same calendar day each week (fixed 168 hours)
parameters.no_rate_combining: employer need not combine more than one overtime rate for the same hour (WO16 §3(D))
parameters.hours_counted: hours actually worked (paid sick/holiday hours not worked do not count)

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001); age 18+ and 16-17 year olds not required to attend school
rules.quote: One and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay for all hours worked in excess of eight hours up to and including 12 hours in any workday, and for the first eight hours worked on the seventh consecutive day of work in a workweek; and
rules.notes: Collective bargaining agreements meeting the 30%-above-minimum-wage test are exempt from WO16 §3(A)-(E) (see cba-hours-meal-exemption-30-percent). Public works have separate overtime rules (Labor Code 1810-1815).

rules.title: Double time after 12 hours/day and after 8 hours on the 7th consecutive day
rules.plain_english: Pay double the regular rate for hours over 12 in a workday and for hours over 8 on the seventh consecutive day of work in the workweek.
rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: Double the employee's regular rate of pay for all hours worked in excess of 12 hours in any workday and for all hours worked in excess of eight on the seventh consecutive day of work in a workweek.

rules.title: How to compute the regular rate for overtime
rules.plain_english: Overtime is paid on the 'regular rate', which includes hourly pay plus shift differentials, piece pay, commissions and non-discretionary bonuses. With two or more rates in a week, use a weighted average; for non-exempt salaried workers divide weekly salary by 40.

parameters.multiple_rates: regular_rate = total_week_earnings / total_week_hours (including OT hours); OT premium added on top
parameters.flat_sum_nondiscretionary_bonus: bonus / maximum legal regular hours in bonus period, then 1.5x or 2x for OT hours
parameters.production_bonus: bonus / total hours worked in period; add 0.5x (or 1x for double time) per OT hour
excluded: pay for non-working time (vacation, holiday, illness)
parameters.floor: regular rate may never be less than applicable minimum wage

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.citation: Labor Code 510; IWC Order 16-2001 §3(A)(1)(c); DLSE Overtime FAQ Q1, Q3, Q4
rules.quote: If you are paid two or more rates by the same employer during the workweek, the regular rate is the "weighted average" which is determined by dividing your total earnings for the workweek, including earnings during overtime hours, by the total hours worked during the workweek, including the overtime hours.
rules.notes: Meal/rest premiums are paid at the 'regular rate of compensation' (Ferra v. Loews, 2021 - case law, not read here).

rules.title: Overtime may be paid on the next regular payday
rules.plain_english: Overtime earned in one pay period must be paid no later than the payday for the next regular pay period. Straight-time wages cannot be delayed.

parameters.deadline: payday of the next regular payroll period after the period in which OT was earned
parameters.wage_statement_correction: OT hours may be recorded as a correction on the next itemized statement with the dates corrected

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Overtime wages must be paid no later than the payday for the next regular payroll period following the payroll period in which the overtime wages were earned.

rules.title: All hours 'suffered or permitted' must be paid, even unauthorized overtime
rules.plain_english: If the employer knew or should have known the employee was working, the time must be paid, including overtime that was not approved. The employer may discipline for breaking the policy but must still pay. Overtime pay cannot be waived.

parameters.hours_worked_definition: time subject to employer control, including all time suffered or permitted to work (WO16 §2(J))

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.citation: Labor Code 1194; IWC Order 16-2001 §2(J); DLSE Overtime FAQ Q2, Q9
rules.quote: California's wage and hour laws require that the employee be compensated for any hours he or she is "suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so."
rules.notes: Relevant to timekeeping checks: pre-shift tailgate meetings, yard time and loading tools are typically hours worked when required by the employer.

rules.title: Alternative workweek: up to 10 regular hours/day in construction
rules.plain_english: With a properly adopted alternative workweek schedule, construction employees can work up to 10 hours a day (within 40 hours a week) without daily overtime. Hours beyond the schedule or over 40 still get 1.5x, and over 12 hours gets 2x.

parameters.ot_1_5x: hours beyond regularly scheduled AWS hours and over 40/week
parameters.ot_2x: over 12 hours/day and over 8 hours on days beyond the regularly scheduled workdays
parameters.public_works: AWS requiring >8 hours/day may not be used on public works in violation of Labor Code 1810-1815

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: The alternative workweek schedule shall provide for work by the affected employees of no longer than ten (10) hours per day within a 40 hour workweek without the payment to the affected employees of an overtime rate of compensation pursuant to this section.
rules.notes: Valid only if adopted by the election procedure in WO16 §3(C).

rules.title: Alternative workweek adoption and repeal election steps
rules.plain_english: To adopt an alternative workweek, the employer must propose it in writing, hold disclosure meetings at least 14 days before, win a secret ballot by two-thirds of the work unit, wait 30 days before requiring the new hours, and report the results to DIR within 30 days and post them at the jobsite.

parameters.approval_vote: at least 2/3 of affected employees in the work unit
parameters.ballot: secret ballot during regular hours at work site, before work is performed
parameters.report_to: DIR Office of the Director - Research, P.O. Box 420603, San Francisco, CA 94142-0603
parameters.work_unit: all nonexempt employees of one employer within a given craft who share a common work site

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: adopted in a secret ballot election, held before the performance of work, by at least a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the affected employees in the work unit.
rules.notes: Failure to make the written disclosure/meetings makes the election null and void. Do not send ballots to DIR; only results.

rules.title: No discipline for refusing more than 72 hours in a workweek
rules.plain_english: An employee cannot be fired or disciplined for refusing to work more than 72 hours in a workweek, except in a genuine emergency.

parameters.exception: emergency = unpredictable or unavoidable occurrence at unscheduled intervals requiring immediate action (WO16 §2(F))

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: No employee shall be terminated, disciplined or otherwise discriminated against for refusing to work more than 72 hours in any workweek, except in an emergency as defined in Section 2(F) above.

rules.title: Employee-requested makeup time: no daily OT up to 11 hours
rules.plain_english: If an employee asks in writing to make up time lost for a personal obligation in the same workweek, the makeup hours do not trigger daily overtime unless the day goes over 11 hours or the week over 40.
rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001) (also applies under CBA unless CBA says otherwise)
rules.quote: the hours of that makeup work time, if performed in the same workweek in which the work time was lost, may not be counted toward computing the total number of hours worked in a day for purposes of the overtime requirements, except for hours in excess of 11 hours of work in one (1) day or forty (40) hours of work in one (1) workweek.

rules.title: One day's rest in seven (may accumulate in construction)
rules.plain_english: Employees are entitled to one day of rest in seven. In construction, rest days may be accumulated when the job reasonably requires 7+ straight days, but each calendar month must still include the equivalent of one day off in seven. Employees cannot be disciplined for refusing the 7th day.

parameters.accumulation_allowed: when nature of employment reasonably requires 7+ consecutive days

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.citation: Labor Code 551-552; IWC Order 16-2001 §3(G); DLSE Overtime FAQ Q6
rules.quote: in each calendar month, the employee shall receive the equivalent of one (1) day’s rest in seven (7).
rules.notes: Seventh-consecutive-day overtime rates still apply.

rules.title: Union CBA exemption from overtime/meal rules requires pay 30% above minimum wage
rules.plain_english: Wage Order 16 overtime, alternative workweek and meal period sections do not apply to employees under a valid union agreement that sets wages, hours and conditions, pays premium rates for all overtime, and pays at least 30% more than the state minimum wage ($21.97/hour in 2026).

still_applies: §3(F) makeup time unless CBA says otherwise
§5 reporting time unless CBA says otherwise
requirements: valid CBA expressly providing wages, hours of work and working conditions
premium wage rates for all overtime hours

rules.applies_to: Union-represented construction employees
rules.quote: if the agreement provides premium wage rates for all overtime hours worked and a regular hourly rate of pay for those employees of not less than thirty (30) percent more than the state minimum wage. (See Labor Code Section 514).

rules.title: 30-minute meal period before end of 5th hour
rules.plain_english: An employee working more than 5 hours must get an uninterrupted, duty-free 30-minute meal period starting no later than the end of the 5th hour. It can be waived by mutual consent only if the whole day is 6 hours or less.

parameters.latest_start: end of 5th hour of work (before start of 6th hour)
parameters.required_to_stay_on_premises: then meal period must be paid

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: No employer shall employ any person for a work period of more than five (5) hours without a meal period of not less than thirty (30) minutes, except that when a work period of not more than six (6) hours will complete the day’s work the meal period may be waived by mutual consent of employer and employee.
rules.notes: Timing rule (end of 5th/10th hour) is from the DLSE Meal Periods FAQ citing Brinker (2012). Unpaid if fully relieved of duty.

rules.title: Second 30-minute meal period before end of 10th hour
rules.plain_english: An employee working more than 10 hours must get a second 30-minute meal period starting by the end of the 10th hour. It can be waived only if the day is 12 hours or less and the first meal was not waived.
rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: An employer may not employ an employee for a work period of more than ten (10) hours per day without providing the employee with a second meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total hours worked is no more than twelve (12) hours, the second meal period may be waived by mutual consent of employer and employee only if the first meal period was not waived.

rules.title: On-duty (paid) meal period needs written, revocable agreement
rules.plain_english: A paid on-the-job meal period is allowed only if the nature of the work truly prevents relief from all duty and there is a written agreement that the employee can revoke in writing at any time.

parameters.test: objective: any employee in that job would be prevented from being relieved of all duty

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.citation: Labor Code 512; IWC Order 16-2001 §10(D); DLSE Meal Periods FAQ
rules.quote: An “on duty” meal period shall be permitted only when the nature of the work prevents employee from being relieved of all duty and when, by written agreement between the parties, an on-the-job paid meal period is agreed to and complies with Labor Code Section 512.
rules.notes: The revocation-in-writing statement requirement is stated in the DLSE Meal Periods FAQ.

rules.title: Missed meal period: 1 extra hour of pay per workday
rules.plain_english: If a compliant meal period is not provided, the employer owes the employee one additional hour of pay at the regular rate of compensation for that workday.

parameters.unit: per workday the meal period is not provided

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: If an employer fails to provide an employee a meal period in accordance with the applicable provisions of this order, the employer shall pay the employee one (1) hour of pay at the employee’s regular rate of compensation for each workday that the meal period is not provided.
rules.notes: DLSE: premium is not hours worked for OT and has a 3-year limitations period (Murphy v. Kenneth Cole). DLSE late-payment FAQ: premiums are wages subject to Labor Code 210 (Naranjo 2022). Where a CBA has a final and binding dispute mechanism for meal periods, the CBA prevails.

rules.title: Paid 10-minute rest break per 4 hours or major fraction
rules.plain_english: Employees get a paid, duty-free 10-minute rest break for every 4 hours worked or major fraction (more than 2 hours). No break is required if the day is under 3.5 hours. Typical: 3.5-6 hours = 1 break, over 6-10 = 2, over 10-14 = 3.

parameters.formula: if h < 3.5: 0 else floor(h/4) + (1 if (h - 4*floor(h/4)) > 2 else 0)
parameters.timing: insofar as practicable in the middle of each work period

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.citation: IWC Order 16-2001 §11(A),(C); DLSE Rest Periods FAQ
rules.quote: The authorized rest period time shall be based on the total hours worked daily at the rate of ten (10) minutes net rest time for every four (4) hours worked, or major fraction thereof.
rules.notes: 'Major fraction' = more than 2 hours per DLSE Rest Periods FAQ. Rest periods need not be recorded (WO16 §6(A)(1)). CBA providing equivalent protection is exempt (§11(E)).

rules.title: Construction: rest breaks may be staggered and taken at the immediate work area
rules.plain_english: Construction employers may stagger rest breaks or schedule them to match natural breaks in the work, and may designate the employee's immediate work area as the rest location.

parameters.rest_location: employer-designated areas, may include or be limited to the immediate work area

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: Nothing in this provision shall prevent an employer from staggering rest periods to avoid interruption in the flow of work and to maintain continuous operations, or from scheduling rest periods to coincide with breaks in the flow of work that occur in the course of the workday.
rules.notes: Employees must still be relieved of all duty during the break (Augustus v. ABM, per DLSE FAQ).

rules.title: Missed rest break for continuous operations: make up same day or pay 10 minutes same pay period
rules.plain_english: If stopping would jeopardize the product or process (e.g., a continuous concrete pour), the rest break can be skipped, but it must be made up the same workday or the 10 minutes must be paid at the regular rate in the same pay period.

parameters.condition: limited circumstances where disruption of continuous operations would jeopardize the product or process

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: Rest periods need not be authorized in limited circumstances when the disruption of continuous operations would jeopardize the product or process of the work. However, the employer shall make up the missed rest period within the same workday or compensate the employee for the missed ten (10) minutes of rest time at his/her regular rate of pay within the same pay period.

rules.title: Missed rest break(s): 1 extra hour of pay per workday
rules.plain_english: If any required rest break is not authorized and permitted, the employer owes one additional hour of pay at the regular rate for that workday (one hour per day, not per missed break).
rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: Thus, if an employer does not provide all of the rest periods required in a workday, the employee is entitled to one additional hour of pay for that workday, not one additional hour of pay for each rest period that was not provided during that workday.
rules.notes: A day with both a missed meal and missed rest break can carry two premiums (one each) - case law, not read here.

rules.title: Construction sites must provide potable water, soap and single-use towels for hand washing
rules.plain_english: Construction employers must supply enough drinkable water, soap (or similar cleanser) and single-use towels for hand washing. Unlike other wage orders, a designated eating place is not required.

required_items: adequate supply of potable water
soap or other suitable cleansing agent
single use towels

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: In all places of employment the employer shall provide an adequate supply of potable water, soap, or other suitable cleansing agent and single use towels for hand washing.
rules.notes: Cal/OSHA sanitation and drinking water rules (Title 8) add further requirements (safety domain).

rules.title: Lactation break time and space; $100/day citation
rules.plain_english: Employers must give reasonable break time and a suitable space to express breast milk. Denial can cost one hour of premium pay per violation and a $100-per-day citation.

parameters.break_time: reasonable, each time needed; runs concurrently with rest breaks if possible
parameters.extra_break_time_paid: not required if beyond authorized rest time

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: BOFE may issue a citation for one hundred dollars ($100) for each day an employee is denied reasonable break time or adequate space to express milk.
rules.notes: Space requirements for construction sites (Labor Code 1031) not read in this pass.

rules.title: Missed heat-illness cool-down (recovery) period: 1 hour premium pay
rules.plain_english: A 'recovery period' is a cool-down break to prevent heat illness. If an employer fails to provide one required by a Cal/OSHA standard, it owes one extra hour of pay at the regular rate for that workday, and cool-down time is paid time.

parameters.trigger: recovery period required by Cal/OSHA standard (e.g., 8 CCR 3395) not provided

rules.applies_to: Employers with outdoor (and indoor heat) workers covered by Cal/OSHA heat illness standards, including construction
rules.source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.7 (not fetched; blocked) - text seen only in search excerpts
rules.quote: "recovery period" means a cooldown period afforded an employee to prevent heat illness.
rules.notes: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov blocked automated fetching; quote and premium rule taken from search-result excerpts of Labor Code 226.7 and law-firm summaries. Verify the current statute text.

rules.title: Allow and encourage cool-down rest in shade (at least 5 minutes)
rules.plain_english: Outdoor workers must be allowed and encouraged to take a cool-down rest in the shade of at least 5 minutes whenever they feel they need it, and must be monitored during it.

parameters.trigger: whenever the worker feels the need to protect from overheating
parameters.symptoms_observed: do not order back to work; observe until symptoms abate; provide first aid/EMS

rules.applies_to: All outdoor places of employment, including construction sites
rules.quote: The employer is required to allow and encourage workers to take a cool-down rest in the shade for a period of no less than five minutes at a time when they feel the need to do so to protect themselves from overheating.
rules.notes: Shade/temperature triggers and full heat-plan duties belong to the Cal/OSHA safety domain. Page dated June 2024.

rules.title: Construction is a high-heat industry: extra procedures at 95°F
rules.plain_english: When it is 95°F or hotter, construction employers must follow Cal/OSHA's additional high-heat procedures (e.g., observation, pre-shift meetings).

industries: Transportation/delivery of agricultural products and of construction or other heavy materials

rules.applies_to: Outdoor construction employers
rules.quote: In addition, the following industries are subject to additional requirements in high heat (temperature that equals or exceeds 95 F)
rules.notes: Construction is listed as one of the industries on the same page. Details of 3395(e) procedures belong to the Cal/OSHA domain.

rules.title: Reporting time pay: half the scheduled day, minimum 2 and maximum 4 hours
rules.plain_english: If an employee reports to the jobsite as required but is sent home or given less than half the scheduled day, pay half the scheduled day (at least 2, at most 4 hours) at the regular rate, unless the cause was threats, utility failure, or an Act of God or other cause outside the employer's control.

parameters.rate: regular rate, not below minimum wage
exceptions: threats to employees or property, or civil authorities recommend not working
public utilities fail to supply electricity, water or gas, or failure of utilities or sewer
Act of God or other cause not within employer's control
parameters.cba: applies unless CBA expressly provides otherwise

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: Each workday that an employee is required to report to the work site and does report, but is not put to work or is furnished less than half of his/her usual or scheduled day’s work, the employer shall pay him/her for half the usual or scheduled day’s work, but in no event for less than two (2) hours nor more than four (4) hours at the employee’s regular rate of pay
rules.notes: Weather: rain-outs may fall under 'Act of God' exception - fact specific. WO16 §5 does not contain the separate 'second reporting' 2-hour rule that appears in Orders 1-15 and in the generic DLSE FAQ; do not apply it to WO16 employees without verification. DLSE: not applicable to paid standby or regularly scheduled shifts under 2 hours.

rules.title: Travel after the first required location is paid time
rules.plain_english: Once an employee reaches the first place the employer requires them to be (e.g., the yard or first jobsite), later employer-required travel (yard to jobsite, jobsite to jobsite) must be paid, at overtime rates if it pushes hours over the thresholds.

parameters.trigger: travel occurring after the first location where employee's presence is required by employer
parameters.rate: regular rate or overtime premium where Labor Code 510 / WO16 §3 thresholds are exceeded

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: All employer-mandated travel that occurs after the first location where the employee’s presence is required by the employer shall be compensated at the employee’s regular rate of pay or, if applicable, the premium rate that may be required by the provisions of Labor Code Section 510 and Section 3, Hours and Days of Work, above.

rules.title: Paid sick leave: at least 40 hours or 5 days per year
rules.plain_english: Employers must let employees use at least 40 hours or 5 days of paid sick leave per year, whichever is more (a worker on 10-hour days gets 50 hours).

parameters.rule: greater of 40 hours or 5 x normal shift length
parameters.year: calendar, fiscal, anniversary, or other 12-month period chosen by employer
parameters.local_ordinance: follow more generous local ordinance except preempted topics (lending, paystubs, calculation, notice, payment timing, termination payout)
purposes_include: own or family member's illness, diagnosis, care, treatment, preventive care
jury duty and court appearance as witness (from 2025-01-01)

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Starting on January 1, 2024, an employer must allow an employee to use at least five days or 40 hours, whichever is more (refer to DLSE Opinion Letter 2015.08.07).
rules.notes: DLSE FAQ updated December 31, 2025. Some purposes depend on employer size (25+ employees for certain family-member violence-related uses).

rules.title: Sick leave eligibility: 30 days worked in a year; usable after 90 days
rules.plain_english: An employee who works at least 30 days within a year for the same employer in California is covered (including part-time and temporary). They can start using sick leave after their 90th day of employment.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: All employees who work at least 30 days for the same employer within a year in California, including part-time, per diem, in-home supportive services (IHSS) providers, and temporary employees, are covered by this law with some narrow exceptions.
rules.notes: The 90-day employment period before use is stated on the same DLSE page. Employer may advance leave earlier.

rules.title: Sick leave accrual: 1 hour per 30 worked, or 24 hours by day 120 and 40 by day 200
rules.plain_english: Under an accrual plan, employees earn at least 1 hour of sick leave per 30 hours worked. Other schedules are allowed if the employee has 24 hours by the 120th day and 40 hours by the 200th day. Alternatively, frontload 40 hours/5 days each year.

parameters.frontload_option: 40 hours/5 days available at start of each 12-month period; new hires 24h/3 days by day 120 and 40h/5 days by day 200

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: must earn at least one hour of paid sick leave for each 30 hours of work (the 1:30 schedule). Although employers may adopt or keep other types of accrual schedules (other than 1:30), the schedule must result in an employee having at least 24 hours of accrued sick leave or paid time off by the 120th calendar day of employment and 40 hours by the 200th calendar day of employment.
rules.notes: Exempt employees are deemed to work 40 hours/week for accrual unless normal week is less (statutory detail not read).

rules.title: Sick leave caps: use capped at 40h/5 days; accrual capped at 80h/10 days
rules.plain_english: An employer may limit sick leave use to 40 hours or 5 days a year and may cap total accrued balance at 80 hours or 10 days. Unused accrued leave carries over.

parameters.cap_rule: whichever is more of hours vs. days

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: the law allows employers to limit an employee’s use of paid sick leave to 40 hours or five days during a year. The law also allows an employer to limit an employee’s total accrued paid sick leave to no more than 80 hours or ten days.

rules.title: Sick leave minimum increment may not exceed 2 hours
rules.plain_english: Employees choose how much sick leave to use; the employer may set a minimum increment of no more than 2 hours. Requests may be oral or written, and leave cannot be conditioned on finding a replacement or solely on a doctor's note.

parameters.notice: advance if foreseeable; as soon as practicable if not

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: An employer can set a reasonable minimum amount of hours for each time an employee takes paid sick leave, not to exceed two hours.

rules.title: Sick pay due by next regular payday; rate calculation
rules.plain_english: Sick leave taken must be paid no later than the next regular payday. Non-exempt workers are paid their regular non-overtime rate for the week of use, or the 90-day average method.

parameters.pay_deadline: payday for the next regular payroll period after leave was taken
nonexempt_rate_methods: regular non-overtime rate for the workweek the leave was used
total non-OT compensation in prior 90 days / non-OT hours in full pay periods of prior 90 days
parameters.exempt_rate: same as other forms of paid leave

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: The paid sick leave law requires that an employer provide payment for sick leave taken by an employee no later than the payday for the next regular payroll period after the sick leave was taken.

rules.title: Show sick leave balance on pay stub; keep sick leave records 3 years
rules.plain_english: The available sick leave balance must appear on the pay stub or a document given the same day as pay ('unlimited' is allowed for unlimited plans). Records of sick leave earned and used must be kept for 3 years.

parameters.records: hours (days) accrued and used per employee

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Employers must show how many days of sick leave you have available on your pay stub, or on a document issued the same day as your paycheck.
rules.notes: 3-year record retention stated in the next sentence of the same DLSE FAQ answer.

rules.title: No sick leave payout at termination; restore if rehired within 12 months
rules.plain_english: Unused sick leave does not have to be paid out when employment ends (unless policy says so or it is PTO), but it must be reinstated if the employee is rehired within 12 months.

parameters.exception: PTO covering sick leave that was paid out at separation need not be restored

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: The paid sick leave law requires that your accrued and unused sick leave be restored to you if you return to the same employer within 12 months from the previous separation.
rules.notes: If the employer uses a combined PTO/vacation policy, vested PTO must be paid at separation as vacation (Labor Code 227.3).

rules.title: Construction CBA exemption from paid sick leave law
rules.plain_english: Construction employees covered by a union agreement with specified provisions are fully exempt from the state paid sick leave law. Other qualifying CBAs (paid leave, OT premiums, pay at least 30% above minimum wage) are only partially exempt and must still follow anti-retaliation and use rules.

parameters.construction_cba_fully_exempt: if CBA meets Labor Code 245.5 construction criteria (not read)

must_provide: paid sick days or PTO usable for sick purposes
premium rates for all OT hours

rules.applies_to: Union-represented construction employees
rules.quote: Employees in the construction industry covered by a collective bargaining agreement with specified provisions.
rules.notes: The DLSE FAQ lists this as a full exemption but does not spell out the construction-CBA criteria in Labor Code 245.5(a)(2); the statute could not be read (leginfo blocked). Verify before treating any CBA as exempt.

rules.title: Post the paid sick leave poster; include sick leave terms in 2810.5 notice
rules.plain_english: Display the Labor Commissioner's paid sick leave poster where employees can read it during the workday, and give each nonexempt employee the 2810.5 Notice to Employee that states the sick leave terms.

parameters.poster: Labor Commissioner Paid Sick Leave poster (2026 update)
poster_must_state: right to accrue, request and use paid sick days
right to file complaint with Labor Commissioner

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Employers are required to display a poster in an area frequented by employees where it may be easily read during the workday.

rules.title: Paid sick leave violation penalties
rules.plain_english: Withholding sick pay can cost the greater of three times the sick pay withheld or $250 (capped at $4,000), plus administrative penalties of $50 per day per affected employee up to $4,000 for other violations.

parameters.withheld_sick_pay_penalty: greater of 3 x value of sick days withheld or $250
parameters.state_penalty_trigger: prompt compliance not forthcoming and Labor Commissioner must take additional enforcement action, incl. civil action (per DLSE Manual 30.8)
parameters.source_of_restructured_values: DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual 30.7-30.8 (Dec 2017); statute not read

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.notes: Figures from search-result excerpts (Justia copy of 248.5) and Seyfarth summary; the trigger for the $50/day penalty was not confirmed. Verify the statute before using in calculations.
rules.correction: Status stays unverifiable. The DLSE manual describes the $50/day amount differently from the rule. The $50 per day (or part of a day) is employee damages when a violation causes other harm, such as discharge or retaliation. Separately, a $50 per day, per employee penalty goes to the State when the employer does not comply promptly and the Labor Commissioner must take further enforcement action. The rule merged these into one "administrative_penalty". The manual also gives 10% interest and a $100 penalty for willful posting violations. Its aggregate caps are garbled ("$8,000, $4000 ... and $4,000"), so the $4,000 caps remain unconfirmed. Parameters restructured with per-source labels.

rules.title: Itemized wage statement (pay stub): 9 required items
rules.plain_english: Each payday (or semimonthly) give employees a pay stub showing: gross wages, total hours, piece units and rates, all deductions, net pay, pay period dates, employee name and last 4 of SSN (or ID), employer legal name and address, and every hourly rate with hours at each rate. Also show available sick leave.

parameters.frequency: semimonthly or at each payment of wages (check, cash, or otherwise)
required_items: gross wages earned
total hours worked (not for salaried overtime-exempt)
number of piece-rate units earned and applicable piece rates
all deductions (employee-authorized may be aggregated as one item)
net wages earned
inclusive dates of the pay period
employee name and last four digits of SSN or an employee ID number
name and address of the legal entity that is the employer
all applicable hourly rates in effect and hours worked at each rate
parameters.form: detachable part of check or separate writing

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Pursuant to Labor Code Section 226(a), semimonthly or every time you are paid your wages, whether by check, in cash, or otherwise, you must be given a detachable part of the check or a separate writing showing required information.
rules.notes: List of items is from the DLSE Paydays FAQ (which also links sample hourly and piece-rate stubs). Labor Code 226(a) also requires the employer to keep copies for at least 3 years (statute not read). Piece-rate employees also need rest/recovery and nonproductive time lines under Labor Code 226.2 (not read).

rules.title: Pay stub violation penalties ($50 / $100 per pay period, max $4,000)
rules.plain_english: An employee injured by a knowing and intentional pay stub violation can recover the greater of actual damages or $50 for the first pay period and $100 for each later pay period, up to $4,000, plus attorney's fees.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.notes: Amounts consistent across multiple secondary sources in search results; statute not read. Separate civil penalties under Labor Code 226.3 were reported inconsistently by sources (one: $250 initial / $1,000 subsequent per employee per violation) - not included as a rule.

rules.title: Payroll and time records: required fields, keep 3 years
rules.plain_english: Keep accurate records for every employee (name, address, occupation, SSN, birth date if a minor, daily start/stop times, meal periods, total daily hours, wages and rates, piece-rate details) in English and ink, at the jobsite or a central location, for at least 3 years.

parameters.location: place of employment or central location
parameters.format: English, ink or other indelible form, dated with month/day/year
required_fields: date of birth if under 18 and minor designation
time records of when each work period begins and ends
total wages paid each payroll period incl. value of board/lodging
total hours worked in payroll period and applicable rates
piece rates or incentive plan explanation; accurate production record
need_not_record: meal periods during which operations cease
parameters.public_works: Labor Code 1776 certified payroll requirements also apply

rules.applies_to: Nonexempt employees in on-site construction, drilling, logging and mining occupations (IWC Wage Order 16-2001)
rules.quote: The employer who has control over wages, hours, or working conditions shall also keep said records on file at the place of employment or at a central location for at least three years.
rules.notes: Records must be available to the employee on reasonable request.

rules.title: Produce payroll records within 21 calendar days of request ($750 penalty)
rules.plain_english: When a current or former employee asks (orally or in writing) to inspect or copy their payroll records, the employer must comply within 21 calendar days or owe a $750 penalty.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Your payroll records must be made available to you upon reasonable request, which request must be complied with by your employer as soon as practicable, but no later than 21 calendar days from the date you make such request.

rules.title: Personnel file: inspection/copy within 30 days of written request; keep 3 years
rules.plain_english: Keep each employee's personnel records at least 3 years and let a current or former employee inspect or get a copy within 30 calendar days of a written request (copy cost only). Failure: $750 penalty.

parameters.copy_charge: not more than actual cost of reproduction

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: The employer must make the employee’s personnel records available within 30 calendar days from the date the employer receives a written request for inspection.
rules.notes: CBA exception exists if CBA meets 30%-above-minimum-wage and inspection-procedure criteria.
rules.correction: The retention period runs from termination. Personnel records must be kept "not less than three years after termination of employment", which the rule's unqualified "retention_years: 3" left ambiguous. Replaced it with retention_years_after_termination = 3 and added the one-request-per-year limit for former employees. The 30-day inspection and copy deadlines, written request, $750 penalty, cost-of-reproduction charge, exclusions and CBA exception are confirmed.

rules.title: Give copies of any signed employment document on request
rules.plain_english: On request, give an employee or job applicant a copy of anything they signed relating to getting or keeping the job.

parameters.trigger: request from employee or applicant
parameters.scope: any instrument signed relating to obtaining or holding employment

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Employers are required to give an employee or job applicant, upon request, a copy of any instrument that the employee or applicant has signed relating to the obtaining or holding of employment.

rules.title: Final pay due immediately on discharge or layoff
rules.plain_english: When an employee is fired or laid off (including at the end of a project), all wages, including accrued vacation, are due immediately at the time of termination, at the place of termination.

includes: accrued unused vacation/PTO at final rate

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: An employee who is discharged must be paid all of his or her wages, including accrued vacation, immediately at the time of termination.
rules.notes: Direct deposit authorization terminates at separation unless employee voluntarily authorizes it for final pay and Labor Code 213(d) is met.

rules.title: Final pay on quitting with 72+ hours' notice: due on last day
rules.plain_english: If an employee gives at least 72 hours' notice and quits on that date, all wages including vacation are due at the time of quitting.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: An employee without a written employment contract for a definite period of time who gives at least 72 hours prior notice of his or her intention to quit, and quits on the day given in the notice, must be paid all of his or her wages, including accrued vacation, at the time of quitting.
rules.notes: If the employer cuts the notice short and ends employment earlier, it becomes a discharge: pay immediately.

rules.title: Final pay on quitting without notice: within 72 hours
rules.plain_english: If an employee quits without 72 hours' notice, final wages are due within 72 hours. The employee may ask for the check to be mailed; the mailing date counts as the payment date.

parameters.place_if_not_mailed: employer office in the county where work was performed (Labor Code 208)

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: An employee without a written employment contract for a definite period of time who quits without giving 72 hours prior notice must be paid all of his or her wages, including accrued vacation, within 72 hours of quitting.

rules.title: Oil drilling layoffs: final pay within 24 hours (excluding weekends/holidays)
rules.plain_english: Oil drilling employees who are laid off must be paid within 24 hours, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and holidays.
rules.applies_to: Employers in the business of oil drilling (drilling occupations under Wage Order 16)
rules.quote: An employee engaged in the business of oil drilling who is laid off must be paid within 24 hours after discharge, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays.

rules.title: Waiting time penalty: one day's pay per day late, up to 30 days
rules.plain_english: If final wages are willfully paid late, the employer owes the employee's daily rate of pay for each calendar day they are late, up to 30 days.

parameters.day_type: calendar days including weekends and holidays
parameters.daily_rate: regular hours per day x hourly rate; include overtime only if regularly scheduled each week
stops_accruing: filing a court action (a DLSE claim does not stop it)
parameters.defense: good faith dispute that wages are due (8 CCR 13520)

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: The penalty is measured at the employee's daily rate of pay and is calculated by multiplying the daily wage by the number of days that the employee was not paid, up to a maximum of 30 days.
rules.notes: Unpaid accrued vacation at separation triggers the penalty; unreimbursed expenses do not.

rules.title: Pay all undisputed wages even when some are disputed
rules.plain_english: Even in a dispute, the employer must pay all wages that are not in dispute, with no release or condition. Failing to do so defeats a good-faith defense to waiting time penalties.

parameters.rule: pay undisputed amount unconditionally at the time due

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Even if there is a dispute, the employer must pay, without requiring a release, whatever wages are due and not in dispute.

rules.title: Cannot require a release of wage claims before paying; also CSLB discipline
rules.plain_english: An employer cannot require an employee to sign a release of wage claims unless those wages have actually been paid, or require signing a timesheet the employer knows is false as a condition of pay. Doing so is a misdemeanor and a cause for CSLB license discipline.

parameters.includes: requiring a statement of hours worked the employer knows is false as condition of pay

rules.applies_to: All employers; licensed contractors face CSLB discipline
rules.source: https://www.cslb.ca.gov/Resources/GuidesAndPublications/LawReferenceBook2021.pdf PDF page 892 (Appendix, Labor Code §206.5, 2021 edition); and PDF page 351 of the 2026 CSLB Law Book (B&P §7110.1)
rules.quote: An employer shall not require the execution of a release of a claim or right on account of wages due, or to become due, or made as an advance on wages to be earned, unless payment of those wages has been made.
rules.notes: Labor Code 206.5 text read from the 2021 CSLB Law Book appendix (official CSLB publication; 2026 edition omits the appendix). B&P 7110.1 in the 2026 Law Book: requiring a release in violation of LC 206.5 is a cause for disciplinary action.

rules.title: Vacation is wages: no forfeiture; pay out unused vacation at final rate
rules.plain_english: Earned vacation cannot be forfeited ('use it or lose it' is illegal), though a reasonable accrual cap is allowed. All vested, unused vacation must be paid at the final rate when employment ends.

parameters.payout_at_separation: all vested unused vacation at final rate of pay
parameters.cba_exception: unless a CBA provides otherwise (Labor Code 227.3)

rules.applies_to: Employers that offer paid vacation or PTO
rules.quote: a policy that provides for the forfeiture of vacation pay that is not used by a specified date ("use it or lose it") is an illegal policy under California law and will not be recognized by the Labor Commissioner.
rules.notes: Union construction trades often handle vacation through trust funds under CBAs.

rules.title: Pay at least twice a month: 1st-15th by the 26th; 16th-end by the 10th
rules.plain_english: Most employees must be paid at least twice a month on regular paydays. Wages for the 1st-15th are due by the 26th of the same month; wages for the 16th-end of month are due by the 10th of the next month.

parameters.holiday_rule: if payday falls on a holiday the business observes by closing, pay next business day
parameters.exempt_EAP_option: may be paid once a month on or before the 26th if full month's salary (incl. unearned portion) is paid
parameters.timecard_not_submitted: must still pay wages reasonably known to be due on payday

rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Wages earned between the 1st and 15th days, inclusive, of any calendar month must be paid no later than the 26th day of the month during which the labor was performed, and wages earned between the 16th and last day of the month must be paid by the 10th day of the following month.

rules.title: Weekly/biweekly payroll: pay within 7 calendar days after period ends
rules.plain_english: For weekly, biweekly or other pay periods that are not the 1st-15th / 16th-end split, pay within 7 calendar days after the end of the pay period.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: Other payroll periods such as weekly, biweekly (every two weeks) or semimonthly (twice per month) when the earning period is something other than between the 1st and 15th, and 16th and last day of the month, must be paid within seven calendar days of the end of the payroll period within which the wages were earned.

rules.title: Post a payday notice (day, time, place of payment)
rules.plain_english: Post a notice showing the regular paydays and the time and place of payment. An employer-made notice is fine. Not posting it, or not paying on payday, is a misdemeanor.
rules.applies_to: All California employers (any size) and their nonexempt employees, including construction contractors
rules.quote: The employer must establish a regular payday and is required to post a notice that shows the day, time and location of payment.

rules.title: Late or short pay penalty: $100 first, $200 + 25% subsequent/willful
